acts.title: The regrets people actually report
text: Surveys of what people ___ produce almost the same list every time.
The commonest single answer is choosing the wrong ___ , usually at about twenty.
The second is money, and specifically housing: a great many people remember a year when a flat was just about ___ .
They did not buy it, and they now describe never investing in ___ as their one financial regret.
Others say they ___ investment opportunities they were offered and did not understand.
But the regret that comes top in almost every study is not financial at all: it is not giving enough ___ to the people they lived with.

items.q: I regret not paying into a private ___ early enough.
Why did you turn ___ that job offer?

acts.title: Text A · What people actually regret
text: Ask a large enough group of people what they regret and the answers arrange themselves into three piles.
The first is money, and it is always specific. I wish I had bought a flat in 2009. I wish I had paid into a pension at twenty-five instead of thirty-five. If only I hadn’t turned down that job.

The second is people. This pile is bigger and less comfortable. I wish I had made up after that row. I wish I had visited more often while there was still time. If only I hadn’t said what I said at my sister’s wedding.
The third pile is the interesting one, because almost nothing is in it. Very few people report regretting something they did. Almost everything on the list is something they did not do.

items.q: How do the regrets arrange themselves, according to the text?
o: Into money, people, and a third pile that is nearly empty

items.q: What is the finding about the third pile?
o: People regret what they did not do far more than what they did

acts.title: Text B · Why inaction stays with us
text: There is a reasonable explanation for the imbalance, and it is not that we behave well.

A thing you did has an ending. It went badly, you dealt with it, and the story closes. A thing you did not do has no ending at all: the alternative life stays open, and it improves quietly every year, because nothing ever happens in it to spoil it.
This is why the regret that people report most often is not a disaster. It is a phone call not made, an application not sent, a flat not bought in a year that now looks obvious.
The practical conclusion is uncomfortable. If you find yourself thinking I wish I could, rather than I wish I had, you are still inside the only period when that sentence can be changed.

items.s: The writer says a thing you did has an ending.
The imagined alternative life gets worse over time.
The most commonly reported regrets are disasters.
The writer says an unsent application is a typical regret.
The writer suggests “I wish I could” marks a situation still open.

acts.title: Look again at the two texts
text: I wish I had bought a flat in 2009.
If only I hadn’t said what I said at my sister’s wedding.
I wish I could speak Spanish.
I wish I lived closer to my sister.
I wish people wouldn’t call at nine on a Sunday.
If you find yourself thinking I wish I could, rather than I wish I had…

items.q: “I wish I had bought a flat” — when is this about?
o: The past, and it did not happen

items.q: “I wish I lived closer” — when is this about?
o: Now, and it is not the case

items.q: “I wish people wouldn’t call on a Sunday.” What does wouldn’t express?
o: Irritation at somebody else’s repeated behaviour

items.q: What is the difference between wish and if only?
o: Almost none — if only is more emphatic
if only is about the future

acts.title: wish and if only
rule: wish and if only work exactly like the unreal conditionals of Lesson 45: the tense steps back one further than the time you mean. What makes them harder is that three different structures sit under one word, and each one points at a different thing.
points: About now. It is not true, and you would like it to be. I wish I lived closer.
About the past. It did not happen, and you regret it. I wish I had bought that flat.
About somebody else’s behaviour, and it is always a complaint. I wish he would stop.
About ability now. I wish I could speak Spanish.
You cannot wish would about yourself
I wish I would stop is not English. Use could, or change the sentence.
The same three structures, with more feeling. If only I hadn’t said it.
eg: I wish I lived closer to my sister.
Present. I do not live closer.
I wish I were taller.
Present, with were.
I wish I had bought a flat in 2009.
Past regret.
If only I hadn’t said that.
Past regret, stronger.
I wish I could speak Spanish.
Ability now.
I wish he would stop interrupting.
Complaint about somebody else.
I wish it would stop raining.
Complaint about a situation.
I wish I could stop biting my nails.
Not “I wish I would stop” — use could about yourself.
If only we had known at the time.
Past, formal and regretful.
I wish I had listened to my father.
The single commonest sentence in this whole lesson.
acts.careful: “I wish I would go” is not English. wish + would is only ever used about somebody or something else, and it always carries a complaint.

items.from: I do not live close to my sister, and I would like to.

steps.a: I wish I lived closer to my sister

steps.cue: Now make it a past regret instead: I did not buy the flat in 2009
steps.a: I wish I had bought the flat in 2009
steps.why: wish + past simple is about now; wish + past perfect is about the past.

items.from: He keeps interrupting me and it annoys me.

steps.cue: Rewrite it with WISH and WOULD
steps.a: I wish he would stop interrupting me

steps.cue: Now say the same kind of thing about your own habit — but you cannot use would
steps.a: I wish I could stop biting my nails
steps.why: wish + would is only ever about somebody else.

items.from: I said something at the wedding and I regret it.

steps.cue: Now write the same regret as a THIRD conditional
steps.a: If I hadn’t said it none of this would have happened
alt: If I hadn’t said it, none of this would have happened
If I had not said it none of this would have happened

items.from: I cannot speak Spanish, and I would like to be able to.

steps.cue: Rewrite it with WISH and COULD
steps.a: I wish I could speak Spanish

steps.cue: Now turn it into a regret about not learning it, with WISH and the past perfect
steps.a: I wish I had learned Spanish
alt: I wish I had learnt Spanish

write.q: Write about 180 words on your own regrets and wishes. Include at least two past regrets with wish or if only + past perfect, at least two present wishes with wish + past simple or could, and one complaint about somebody else with wish + would. Then say which of them you could still act on.
write.model:
I wish I had learned to play something. There was a piano in the flat until I was fifteen, my grandmother offered to teach me twice, and I said no on both occasions for reasons I could not now reconstruct.

If only I hadn’t left the university course in the second year. It was a mistake made for a good reason — money — and I have spent eleven years being politely asked about it in interviews.

I wish I lived nearer my parents. Four hours is exactly the distance that makes a Sunday visit impossible and a monthly one feel insufficient.

I wish I could stop checking my phone at traffic lights, which is a smaller thing and a more embarrassing one to admit.

And I wish people wouldn’t ask about the degree.

Of all of these, only two are still open. The phone is entirely within my control. The piano is not gone either — my grandmother is eighty-four and the offer, I suspect, still stands.
